notes:
Audited every buffer allocator in numbduck/duckdb_utils.py against the real duckdb.h struct/handle sizes for the supported range (duckdb>=1.3.2,<1.6). All sizes are correct and none is undersized.

create_duckdb_result() -> allocate_buffer(6) = 48 bytes (duckdb_utils.py:35-37). The duckdb_result struct is 6 pointer-width fields (3x idx_t/uint64 deprecated counts + 3x pointers: deprecated_columns, deprecated_error_message, internal_data) = 48 bytes, stable across 1.3.2-1.5. libduckdb writes the full 48-byte struct through `duckdb_result *out_result`; the 6x int64 buffer exactly covers it. No overflow.

The six handle allocators each -> allocate_buffer(1) = 8 bytes: create_duckdb_connection (:13), create_duckdb_database (:19), create_duckdb_prepared_statement (:25), create_duckdb_data_chunk (:31), create_duckdb_value (:43), create_duckdb_vector (:49). Each corresponding C type is an opaque pointer (typedef struct _x { void *internal_data; } *x), 8 bytes on the supported 64-bit platforms. The `duckdb_X *out_X` out-param receives a single pointer, so 1x int64 = 8 bytes is exactly sufficient.

int64 dtype guarantees 8-byte width and numpy guarantees 8-byte data alignment, satisfying duckdb_result/handle alignment requirements. numpy.zeros zero-initializes (safe). 32-bit is documented unsupported (architecture.md:276); there the 8-byte int64 cells would over-size 4-byte pointers (safe, never undersized). No correctness or memory-safety defect found in buffer sizing. Empty findings is the correct result.
